lines: I.  Introduction
Fig. 4.  Why the rule fails, as five deficits. Each small arm in turn overtakes the dominant one, takes its single sample and resets; the dominant arm gains 17/23 of deficit each time it is skipped.

An adaptive scheme allocates samples across arms, stops when a certificate is available, and must be analysed on three fronts: the probability that its confidence event holds, the expected time at which it stops, and whether its realised counts actually follow the intended proportions. Three claims in that analysis were carried as inputs rather than theorems.

The step from a bound on the tail sum to a bound on the EXPECTED stopping time was cited as standard rather than proved — and high-probability correctness alone gives nothing here, because off the good event the algorithm may never stop at all. And tracking — whether an online rule can realise the intended proportions — was simply open.
What the literature leaves open

The literature therefore leaves a specific opening. The fixed-confidence framework supplies the analysis but carries concentration and layer-cake as inputs; apportionment supplies a general impossibility but no instance an analysis can use; concentration theory supplies the inequality but not its instantiation at the peeling budget.

No existing treatment simultaneously: (i) proves the layer-cake transfer for the N-valued stopping time the analysis needs; (ii) discharges the per-arm concentration input at the peeling budget; (iii) separates per-horizon existence from online achievability by proving the first and refuting the second; and (iv) quantifies how common and how early the online failure is.

III.  Results

THE ONLINE RULE VIOLATES QUOTA AT HORIZON ELEVEN. With targets (17, 1, 1, 3, 1)/23 the largest-deficit rule reaches counts (7, 1, 1, 1, 1) after eleven steps, at which point the first arm's deficit is 26/23 ≈ 1.13, exceeding the per-horizon bound of one. Continuing to horizon fourteen the deficit reaches 31/23 ≈ 1.35.
Over rational targets on three to five arms the worst deficit observed was 31/23, and the first violation appears as early as horizon eleven — so the failure is not asymptotic and not rare.

It is not driven by one corner of the grid: the violating fraction is between 26\ peaking at four arms and declining only slowly thereafter, so more arms neither rescue the bound nor are needed to break it.
IV.  Discussion

THE FAILURE IS COMMON, AND FLAT ACROSS ARM COUNTS. Exhaustive over 1,228,079 rational targets: 375,239 — 30.6% — drive the largest-deficit rule past the bound of one, the worst reaching 7/4 at eight arms.

A CLAIM THIS WORK PREVIOUSLY MADE, AND WHICH IS WRONG. It is tempting to conclude that any rule serving whole samples faces the same arithmetic. Seven rules were run on the same targets, four of them classical apportionment divisor methods. Jefferson's rule violates the deficit bound on ZERO of the 1,228,079 targets — never, not rarely.

The failure can be relocated between the deficit and the surplus directions but not removed, which is what the apportionment impossibility gives and what the sweep confirms without exception. An analysis needing both directions has no rule to appeal to; one needing only the surplus direction may use Jefferson.
Limitations — what is not established

One rule, not all rules. Theorem refutes the bound 1 for this rule. It does not prove that no online monotone rule achieves any constant bound, and the constant for a divisor method is not computed here. The rule-to-counts link is not machine-checked.

Rational targets on three to five arms with denominators to 30, run to horizon 40. Nothing here bounds the worst deficit over all targets, arm counts and horizons, and such a bound — an impossibility with a matching constant — is the natural companion this paper does not supply. A known sub-Gaussian parameter is assumed.
Corollary converts it; establishing it belongs to the algorithm's own analysis.
V.  Conclusions

House monotonicity and quota cannot both hold, and the consequence for an adaptive stopping analysis is concrete: the tracking assumption that the per-horizon deficit stays below one is false for the rule such an analysis would naturally assume, on 30.6% of targets, from t = 3 onwards. The refutation cannot be evaded by changing rules — only relocated.
An analysis requiring two-sided control has nothing to appeal to.
How the numbers were produced
EXHAUSTIVE OVER RATIONAL TARGETS, IN INTEGERS. Every target shares a denominator d, so the deficit t·wᵢ − Nᵢ equals (t·pᵢ − Nᵢ·d)/d and the whole simulation runs in integer arithmetic.

The partition generator produces the identical set on every (K, d) tested, and the rewritten sweep reproduces the earlier rational run field for field — same target count, same violation count, same worst deficit, same earliest horizon. AND THE SWEEP CHECKS ITSELF.
A HORIZON BOUND CAN ONLY UNDERSTATE: running longer can only find more violations, so every count here is a lower bound.
